summary: Specifies procedures for processing IPv6 Hop-by-Hop options in routers and hosts. It modifies the rules in RFC 8200 to make the Hop-by-Hop Options header practical to use, so that such options can be deployed. It updates RFC 8200.

eli5.summary: Some notes on a parcel are meant for every post office along the way. This changes the rules so post offices can read those notes without slowing everything down.

questions: how are ipv6 hop-by-hop options processed
why are ipv6 hop-by-hop options dropped
what is the full forwarding rate
can a router drop packets with hop-by-hop options
subtitle: Updated rules that let IPv6 routers skip Hop-by-Hop options safely instead of dropping or choking on those packets.

tldr.problem: IPv6 Hop-by-Hop options can push packets onto a router's slow path, which invites denial-of-service attacks, so many routers drop such packets and the options are hard to use.
tldr.mechanism: Routers process Hop-by-Hop options only if configured and only at the full forwarding rate, otherwise they skip the options and forward the packet. Unrecognized options with action bits 01, 10 or 11 are now treated much like 00, and new options should be simple and small.
tldr.outcome: The RFC updates RFC 8200 so that a packet is never dropped merely for carrying a Hop-by-Hop Options header, aiming to make these options practical to deploy.

today: RFC 9673 is a Proposed Standard from October 2024 that updates RFC 8200. It has not been obsoleted or updated itself.

sections.title: Why Hop-by-Hop Options Were a Problem
sections.content:
In early IPv6 specifications (RFC 1883, RFC 2460) every node had to process Hop-by-Hop options. That proved impractical in high-speed routers: RFC 7045 observed that such routers will either ignore the options or send those packets to a slow processing path.

The RFC lists the trouble this causes:

  • Options sent to the slow path can degrade the router and be exploited for a denial-of-service (DoS) attack.
  • If only some packets in a flow carry options, packets can be reordered, which hurts upper-layer protocols.
  • Many or large options increase the bytes to process. Measurements show packets are more likely to cross the Internet if the extension header chain is under 40 bytes.
  • Some Internet paths simply drop packets with a Hop-by-Hop Options header.

RFC 8200 had already said nodes should only process the header if explicitly configured to do so, but it was meant to document existing practice, not change it. The main issues remained.
sections.eli5: If every post office had to stop and read every note on every parcel, the mail would crawl, and a prankster could jam the office with notes. So many offices threw such parcels away.

sections.title: Router Terms Used
sections.content:
The RFC uses a few loosely defined terms. The Forwarding Plane moves user and application data by looking at packet headers. The Control Plane handles management and routing information exchanged with other routers. The Fast Path is optimized for forwarding, perhaps in ASICs or a network processor. The Slow Path is general purpose and handles packets that need special processing.

The Full Forwarding Rate is the rate at which a router can forward packets without hurting its aggregate forwarding rate, sometimes called wire speed.
sections.eli5: A router has a fast lane for ordinary parcels and a slow desk for odd ones. The goal is to keep the fast lane moving.

sections.title: Handling the Hop-by-Hop Options Header
sections.content:
The Hop-by-Hop Options header is identified by a Next Header value of 0, must appear immediately after the IPv6 header, and can appear at most once in a packet.

Routers that process it SHOULD use the method in this RFC. Even a router that does not process the header MUST forward the packet normally, and a router MUST NOT drop a packet solely because it carries Hop-by-Hop options. A configuration may control whether any or all of the options are skipped. A router that does not process the header does not process any option in it.

Hosts SHOULD process the header in received packets. A constrained host may not; if so, it MUST process the rest of the packet normally.
sections.eli5: A post office may choose not to read the notes, but it must still deliver the parcel.

sections.title: Processing Individual Options
sections.content:
A source SHOULD be robust to nodes processing only some options, and should put options in decreasing order of importance. A router SHOULD NOT be configured to process the first option if that hurts the aggregate forwarding rate, and SHOULD process further options only if that does not either.

If a router cannot or is not configured to process an option, it SHOULD act as for an unrecognized option with action bits 00 and skip the rest using the Hdr Ext Len field, which gives the header length in 8-octet units. Skipped options need not be verified.

RFC 8200 defines the top two bits of the Option Type as the action for unrecognized options. This RFC loosens the rules for 01, 10 and 11: discarding becomes a MAY, if so configured, and the ICMP Parameter Problem, Code 2 message also becomes a MAY. The ICMP message costs the router work, and is not guaranteed to reach the source.

The Router Alert Option is the exception because it asks for Control Plane processing. A node that processes it MUST protect itself, for example with an access control list or rate limiting, and SHOULD verify that the protocol in the option's Value field is one the router is configured to care about. The set of enabled options SHOULD be configurable by the operator.
sections.eli5: If the post office cannot read a note quickly, it skips it and passes the parcel on. Only the special red-flag note may get a closer look, and the office must guard itself against fake red flags.

sections.title: Rules for New Hop-by-Hop Options
sections.content:
This section updates Section 4.8 of RFC 8200. Future Hop-by-Hop options should be designed to be processed at the Full Forwarding Rate, which means:

  • they should be simple to process;
  • the action bits should be 00, so routers that do not recognize them skip them;
  • their size should not go beyond what can be handled at that rate, since a larger header raises the chance of drops;
  • they should assume a router might process only a subset, such as the first option;
  • protocols using them should assume a router may drop packets containing them.

An option that does not meet these criteria must have a detailed explanation of why it can still proceed at the full forwarding rate.

The RFC also describes robust use: an application can send a test packet carrying the option and only keep using it once that packet is acknowledged, repeating the check from time to time since paths change. This is sometimes called racing.
sections.eli5: If you invent a new kind of note, keep it short and easy to read, and make sure the parcel still works if nobody reads it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The core security issue is that anything forcing packets into a router's Control Plane or Slow Path can be used for DoS by saturating the resources for routing and management protocols. The Router Alert Option is the one option designed for Control Plane processing.

The RFC says the changes significantly reduce the attack surface: routers should not process options they cannot handle at the full rate, the Router Alert Option gets controls, packets with a Hop-by-Hop header are expected to be forwarded, and new options should be cheap and small. Implementations should also fail gracefully on malformed or malicious options, and a very large extension header can stop a router using hardware optimizations such as equal cost multipath forwarding or port filtering.
sections.eli5: Making the slow desk do less work means pranksters have less to jam.

viz.caption: ACTION BITS FOR UNRECOGNIZED OPTIONS (AS MODIFIED)

items.label: Skip
items.desc: Skip the option and continue processing the header.

items.label: May discard
items.desc: MAY discard the packet, if so configured.

items.label: May discard, may send ICMP
items.desc: MAY discard if configured; an ICMP Parameter Problem, Code 2 MAY be sent.

items.label: May discard, ICMP if unicast
items.desc: MAY discard if configured; ICMP MAY be sent if the destination was not multicast.
